ta-l1d14q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus opening Lombard's treatment of the Holy Spirit's temporal procession (Distinctions 14–18). He treats the temporal procession in general (14–15), its special modes of mission (16–17), and the names 'gift' and 'given', which express its character (18). In Distinction 14 he shows that the Spirit proceeds temporally from Father and Son (from Augustine and Bede), and in Distinction 15 asks whether he also gives himself. He refutes those who say that not the Spirit himself, who is God, but only his gifts are given, and concludes that no human, not even Christ as man, can give the Spirit, answering an objection from the Apostle. Thomas announces three inquiries: on the temporal procession in itself, on what it consists in, and on who brings it about. The first has two articles: whether there is a temporal procession of the Spirit, and whether it is counted with the eternal one.
claims: The Spirit himself, not only his gifts, is given in his temporal procession.
No human, not even Christ as man, can give the Holy Spirit.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3532.summary: First objection against a temporal procession of the Spirit. The Spirit's procession is his distinguishing property as generation is the Son's, and generation is called temporal only by the assumed nature. The Spirit assumes no nature, so he has no temporal procession.
claims: The Son's generation is temporal only through the assumed nature.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3535.summary: Second objection. Whatever has something temporally is mutable, which does not fit the Spirit, who is true God.
claims: What has something temporally is mutable.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3538.summary: Third objection from the Liber de causis: between things whose substance and operation are in time and things whose substance and operation are in eternity, such as separate substances and above all God, there are things whose substance is in eternity and operation in time. Procession, active or passive, is an operation of God, so it is not in time.
claims: God's substance and operation are both in eternity.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3542.summary: Fourth objection. What raises a person above time cannot be called temporal, and the Spirit's procession into a person raises them above all temporal things, since insofar as we grasp something eternal with the mind we are not in this world (Augustine).
claims: Grasping the eternal lifts the mind above the world.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3545.summary: Fifth objection. The temporal procession, also called mission, includes the eternal procession (Augustine), and denomination should be from the worthier, so it should be called eternal, not temporal.
claims: Denomination should be from the worthier part.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3548.summary: Notes that the authorities in Lombard's text say the contrary.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3551.summary: Sed contra. Someone may come to have the Spirit in time who did not have him before. The Spirit is had only as proceeding from Father and Son, being the gift of both, so there is a temporal procession by which he proceeds to sanctify the creature.
claims: The Spirit is newly had by creatures as proceeding from Father and Son.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3554.summary: Thomas's determination. Although procession among the divine persons properly means going out from a principle, which need not tend into another, the Spirit's procession, by its mode as love, does tend into another, the beloved, as its object. The eternal processions of the persons are the cause and reason of all creaturely production. As the Son's generation is the reason of all creation, since the Father made all things in the Son, so the Father's love tending to the Son as its object is the reason in which God bestows every effect of love on creatures. The Spirit, the love by which the Father loves the Son, is also the love by which he loves the creature, sharing his perfection with it. So the procession of this love can be considered as tending into the eternal object, the eternal procession, or into a created object, insofar as something is conferred on creatures through this love, the temporal procession. It is called temporal because from the newness of the effect a new relation of the creature to God arises, by reason of which God must be signified under a new relation to the creature, as with everything said of God from time.
claims: The Spirit's procession, as love tending into an object, can be eternal (into the Son) or temporal (into creatures).
The same love by which the Father loves the Son is the love by which he loves creatures.
Temporal procession implies a new relation in the creature, signified of God as from time.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the first objection. Generation by its concept implies a relation only to the one from whom it is. In the Son this can be the one from whom he receives the divine nature, eternal generation from the Father, or the one from whom he receives human nature, temporal generation from the mother. The Spirit's procession implies not only a relation to its principle, by which it is only eternal, but also a relation to that into which it proceeds, by which it can be called temporal.
claims: Generation is relative only to its source; the Spirit's procession is also relative to its object, which allows a temporal procession.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3561.summary: Reply to the second objection. When a gift is conferred on a creature through the love that is the Spirit, no change occurs in the love but in the recipient, if this should be called change rather than perfection. So the temporal relation is posited in the Spirit only conceptually and really in the changed creature, as when God is called Lord from time.
claims: The temporal relation is real only in the creature, conceptual in the Spirit.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3564.summary: Reply to the third objection. Divine operation can be considered on the side of the operator, and then it is eternal, or of its effect, and then it can be temporal. Because God does not act by an operation intermediate between himself and his work, his operation being in him and his whole substance, his operation is essentially eternal and its effect temporal.
claims: God's operation is eternal and identical with his substance; only its effects are temporal.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3567.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. 'Temporal' is said in several ways: as subject to the variation of time, in which sense the procession is not temporal, even in its effect of grace; or as having a beginning in time, in which sense grace is temporal and so is the procession by reason of its effect.
claims: The temporal procession is 'temporal' as having a beginning in time, not as subject to time's variation.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3570.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. A conjunction can be affirmed only if both parts hold but can be denied if either fails, as with a conjunctive proposition. 'Temporal' includes a negation with an affirmation (being at some time and not having been before), while 'eternal' implies only affirmation of being. So a compound can be called eternal only if both parts are eternal, but temporal if one is. Likewise 'Creator' implies divine operation and connotes an actual effect in creatures, so God is called Creator not from eternity but from time.
claims: A compound of eternal and temporal is called temporal, as 'Creator' is said of God from time.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3582.summary: First argument that the temporal procession is counted with the eternal as another procession. Eternal and temporal cannot be the same in essence, and things differing in essence are simply multiplied and counted.
claims: Eternal and temporal differ in essence.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3585.summary: Second argument. Nothing is a sign of itself, and the temporal procession is a sign of the eternal (Augustine).
claims: The temporal procession is a sign of the eternal.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3588.summary: Third argument. The two either differ essentially or one adds to the other. The eternal cannot add to the temporal, which would make the temporal naturally prior; nor can the temporal add to the eternal, since nothing can be added to the perfect eternal. So they differ essentially and are simply two.
claims: Nothing can be added to the eternal.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3592.summary: Fourth argument. The Spirit relates to passive procession as the Son to passive generation, and the Son is said to have two nativities and to be born twice, so the Spirit has two processions.
claims: The Son has two births.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3595.summary: Sed contra. A procession posits something in the one proceeding, but the temporal procession as temporal posits nothing in the Spirit. So it essentially includes the eternal, and they are not simply several.
claims: Temporal procession as such posits nothing in the Spirit.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3598.summary: Second sed contra. Things not of the same character are not counted together, and temporal and eternal are not of the same character.
claims: Things of different character are not counted together.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3601.summary: Thomas's determination. Since procession always implies the relation of the proceeding to its source, and the Spirit is related to the Father only by an eternal relation, no procession of the Spirit is essentially other than the eternal. But another relation can come to him on the side of the one he is in as beloved, and by that it is called temporal. So the procession is one essentially, by the one relation of the proceeding to its source, which it principally implies. It is twofold by reason of two relations to two objects, eternal and temporal. The eternal one is really in the Spirit; the temporal one is only conceptually in the Spirit and really in the one he proceeds into. The first is included in the second as its reason and cause, so the second is by addition to the first.
claims: The Spirit's temporal and eternal procession are essentially one procession, twofold by relation to two objects.
The temporal relation is real in the creature, conceptual in the Spirit, and includes the eternal as its reason.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3604.summary: Reply to the first argument. The procession is called temporal not by what it is but by its relation to the creature.
claims: The procession is temporal only by relation to the creature.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3607.summary: Reply to the second argument. The temporal procession is a sign of the eternal through its effect, from which the temporal relation arises. Its effect is gratuitous love, a likeness of the uncreated love that is the Spirit, and so a sign of it.
claims: Created grace, as likeness of uncreated love, is a sign of the eternal procession.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3611.summary: Reply to the third argument. Nothing can really be added to the eternal, but the eternal can be understood as standing in some relation to something temporal, a relation not really posited in the eternal. Since words are signs of concepts, a name can be imposed on the eternal as understood under that relation, as God is called Lord from time, and so the procession is called temporal.
claims: The eternal can be named under a conceptual relation to the temporal.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3614.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The Son's temporal and eternal generations are distinguished by their principle (eternal from the Father, temporal from the mother) and by the different natures, so one is really not the other. The procession is not like this.
claims: The Son's two generations are really distinct; the Spirit's processions are not.

ta-l1d14q1-d1e3620.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. As relations of the proceeding to its source, the temporal and eternal processions are wholly the same, let alone of the same character, and are not counted. As relations to that into which the procession is, they are of the same character not univocally but analogically, since one is the reason of the other, and so they can be counted together, as we speak of God and a human as two things.
claims: As relations to their objects, eternal and temporal procession are analogically related and can be counted.

ta-l1d14q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 14 opens Lombard's treatment of the Spirit's temporal procession: in general, by special missions, and through the names 'gift' and 'given'. It notes his refutation of those who hold that only the Spirit's gifts are given and his denial that humans can give the Spirit, and announces inquiries into the temporal procession itself, what it consists in, and who brings it about.
claims: The Spirit himself is given in the temporal procession.

ta-l1d14q1-Dd1e3524.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is a temporal procession of the Spirit. Thomas holds that because the Spirit proceeds as love, which tends into the beloved as object, his procession can be eternal (into the Son) or temporal (into creatures). The love by which the Father loves the Son is the love by which he bestows every effect of love on creatures, just as the Son is the reason of all creation. It is temporal because the newness of the effect produces a new relation in the creature, signified of God from time. The Spirit's procession, unlike generation, involves relation to its object. The temporal relation is real only in the creature, God's operation is eternal and only its effect temporal, and the procession is 'temporal' as beginning in time, as 'Creator' is.
claims: There is a temporal procession of the Spirit, by which the same love proceeds into creatures as gift.
The temporal relation is real in the creature, conceptual in the Spirit.

ta-l1d14q1-Dd1e3574.summary: Article 2 asks whether the temporal procession is counted with the eternal. Thomas holds that the procession is essentially one, by the one relation of the Spirit to his source. It is twofold (gemina) by two relations to two objects: the eternal relation, real in the Spirit, and the temporal, real only in the creature and including the eternal as its reason. Created grace is a likeness and sign of uncreated love. Unlike the Son's two really distinct generations, the Spirit's processions are counted only analogically, by relation to their objects.
claims: The Spirit's eternal and temporal processions are one procession, twofold by relation to its objects.
Created grace is a likeness and sign of the Spirit.

ta-l1d14q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 14 begins the treatment of the Spirit's temporal procession. Article 1 holds that because the Spirit proceeds as love tending into the beloved, the same love by which the Father loves the Son proceeds into creatures as the reason of every gift of love. This parallels the Son's role as reason of creation and constitutes a temporal procession, a new relation real only in the creature. Article 2 holds that temporal and eternal procession are essentially one procession, by the Spirit's one relation to his source, and twofold only by relation to eternal and created objects. The temporal includes the eternal as its reason, and created grace is the likeness and sign of uncreated love.
claims: The Spirit proceeds temporally into creatures as the same love by which the Father loves the Son.
Eternal and temporal procession are one procession, twofold by relation to its objects.
Temporal procession posits a new relation only in the creature.
